citation: corpus/herdr-0.8.0/lifecycle/ and corpus/herdr-0.8.0/snapshot/; read out in docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md sections 1 and 10
why: The mirror is the core's picture of daemon truth, and every desideratum above it reads from that picture: which panes exist, what each agent is doing, which one has focus. Its failures are not display bugs. A pane that never disappears is a surface the user cannot close; an agent transition dropped on the floor is the product's whole reason for existing, silently absent. These cases come from a real daemon's recorded event stream rather than from what herdr's docs imply, because three of them describe behavior nobody would have guessed: closing a tab removes its panes with no pane event at all, a pane whose program exits is announced differently from one a client closed, and subscribing replays the entire session as fresh creations. Each case states the whole resulting picture rather than the part it is about, so a change with a side effect somewhere else fails here rather than somewhere later.

cases.name: an empty mirror knows nothing
cases.why: The starting state has to be distinguishable from a real but empty session. A window that renders 'no panes' when it simply has not connected yet is telling the user something false, so health starts disconnected rather than at a hopeful default.

cases.name: a snapshot is the whole world
cases.why: Bootstrap replaces rather than merges. herdr offers no replay, so after any gap the only honest move is to take the new statement entire; merging would preserve entities that died while nobody was watching.

cases.name: subscribing after a snapshot does not double the session
cases.why: The load-bearing case. events.subscribe replays the current session as synthetic creation events, so a client that snapshots and then subscribes is told every existing entity was just created - 7 events for a one-pane session in the recording, 9 for a three-pane one. Convergence is what makes that harmless, and it is a property of the vocabulary rather than a rule each adapter remembers: there is no 'created' event to get wrong, only an upsert.

cases.name: closing a tab takes its panes with it
cases.why: Recorded, and the sharpest trap in the capture: of five panes created, one got pane_closed, one got pane_exited, and two vanished with a parent that announced only itself. A mirror that removes only what it is told about keeps rendering panes whose terminal is gone, and the user has no way to dismiss them. The cascade is the mirror's own inference rather than something the backend said, which is why the change records that it was one.

cases.name: closing a workspace takes its tabs and their panes
cases.why: The same trap one level up, and also recorded: workspace_closed for w2 arrived with no tab_closed for w2:t1 and no pane_closed for w2:p1. Two levels of cascade, so a mirror that handles only the direct children still leaks the panes underneath.

cases.name: a pane whose program exited is removed like any other
cases.why: herdr says pane_exited for a program that ended and pane_closed for a pane a client closed, and never both - the recorded stream goes straight from pane_exited to layout_updated. Muster keeps no such distinction, because both mean the surface should stop existing and keeping the difference would invite handling only one of them. This case pins that one vocabulary word covers both, so the adapter has nowhere to put half the behavior.

cases.name: removing something already gone changes nothing
cases.why: Not defensive coding: it is routine. A reconnect re-snapshots and the replay that follows describes a world the mirror has already caught up with, so a removal for an unknown id arrives in normal operation. Reporting it as a change would repaint for no news; failing on it would take the window down over an event that carried none.

cases.name: an agent state change is reported once, and only when it moves
cases.why: The one change this whole product is about. Reported once so a listener can act on it, and not at all when the state repeats - herdr sends a status event per transition, and a mirror that echoed every one would flash the indicator on no news.

cases.name: a replayed pane does not roll back a live agent state
cases.why:
herdr replays the session as it stood when the subscription opened, and its pane payloads carry agent_status. Letting a structure event write that field makes the backend two writers for it, the replay being the older one, and nothing arrives afterwards to correct the rollback - agent state comes on its own per-pane subscription. A pane stuck showing idle while its agent works is this product failing at the one thing it is for.

The relabel beside it is incidental to that and is still correct: the replayed payload carries a directory the snapshot did not, and what a pane is called is a thing structure events are allowed to write. Only the agent's state is fenced off.

cases.name: detecting a harness renames the pane, and moves nothing else
cases.why: herdr identifies a harness by reading the screen, seconds after the pane started, so a pane is listed before anything knows what is running in it. A list that names panes by their directory and harness would say `src` forever unless this is reported - and on a quiet session nothing else ever comes along to correct it. Reported as a rename rather than as a state change, because an agent that has just been recognized was already doing whatever it was doing.

cases.name: detecting the harness already known reports nothing
cases.why: Detection repeats: herdr re-reads the screen on a timer, and a subscription replays what it already sent. A rename reported every two seconds would republish the whole window forever on a session where nothing is happening, which is the per-event cost the budget is drawn against.

cases.name: a pane that changed directory is renamed
cases.why: A pane is named by the directory it is in, and agents move between them. A row still reading the directory a pane was opened in is a row the user cannot find twice - and unlike a harness, this one changes repeatedly over a session's life.

cases.name: a replayed pane that is the same in every way reports nothing
cases.why: Subscribing replays the whole session, so every pane arrives a second time exactly as it already is. Reporting those as renames would repaint the window on every reconnect, which is the idempotence the whole event model rests on.

cases.name: an agent state for an unknown pane is dropped, not invented
cases.why: An agent event carries a pane id and nothing else - no tab, no workspace. A mirror that created a pane from one would hold an orphan the view cannot place in any tab, which is worse than missing it: the pane would appear nowhere and never leave. The snapshot after a reconnect is what fills real gaps.

cases.name: transitions that ran while nobody was listening are reported on reconnect
cases.why: herdr stamps agent transitions from one session-wide counter, and that stamp reaches a client in exactly one place: the agents[] of a snapshot. It is never on an event. So a gap is visible only by comparing two snapshots against the transitions applied in between - here one was applied and the counter moved by four. Muster exists to route attention, so an agent that asked for the user during the gap has to be surfaced rather than quietly overwritten by the fresh snapshot.

cases.name: a counter that moved by exactly what we applied is not a gap
cases.why: The companion to the case above, because an over-eager gap detector is worse than none: it would claim a missed notification on every ordinary reconnect, and a warning that fires every time is one nobody reads. Two transitions applied, counter up by two, nothing missed.

cases.name: focus cursors are absolute and independent
cases.why: herdr moves three cursors with separate events, each naming only its own. Treating absence as a clear would make a pane focus silently unfocus the workspace. Absolute values are also what makes ordering not matter: two events racing land on the later value rather than compounding.

cases.name: focus does not survive the pane it names
cases.why: A cursor pointing at a removed pane is worse than an empty one: every reader has to handle the dangling case, and the one that forgets renders a pane that is gone. Clearing it here lets the rest of the core treat a focused id as one that exists. The reported change matters as much as the clearing - an earlier version cleared the cursor and told nobody, so a view watching for changes would have kept the stale highlight. The tab goes with it here because it held nothing else, which is the inference below - so this case also shows the two clearings compounding: the pane cursor and then the tab's.

cases.name: a state nobody has heard of reads as unknown, never as idle
cases.why: herdr's API is explicitly unstable and ships weekly, so a newer daemon can name a state this build has never seen. Unknown renders as itself; idle would tell the user nothing needs them, which is the one wrong answer that looks like a right one.

cases.name: a reconnect reports what moved, not that everything did
cases.why: Bootstrap runs again on every reconnection, and a mirror that reported the whole world as new would repaint every pane each time the network hiccupped. What a reader needs is the difference: this pane's agent changed while we were away, that one is gone, this one is new.

cases.name: a tab's tree arrives and is reported once
cases.why: The noun a window renders. herdr sends the whole tab in absolute values on every pane change, so the mirror stores it whole rather than patching it, and reports the tab rather than the tree - every reader already holds the mirror, and only some of them want to walk it.

cases.name: the same tree twice is one change
cases.why: A subscription replays the session it arrived after, and every pane event drags a layout_updated behind it, so a mirror sees the tree it already has constantly. Reporting each one would rebuild every surface in the window for no news, which is the cost the whole change-reporting arrangement exists to avoid.

cases.name: a divider that moved is a change, though the panes did not
cases.why: Someone dragging a divider in herdr's own TUI emits layout_updated with the same panes and a different ratio (observations section 13). A mirror comparing only which panes are present would call that no news, and the window would sit at the old proportions until something else happened to it.

cases.name: a zoomed pane is named, not merely flagged
cases.why: herdr says `zoomed: true` and keeps publishing every pane at its ordinary rect, so a view rendering what it is handed paints the whole tree while the daemon is showing one pane. The adapter resolves the flag against the tab's focused pane, which makes the question a view actually asks - which pane fills this tab - one it cannot answer by accident.

cases.name: closing a tab takes its tree, silently
cases.why: layout_updated fires for every pane change and for no tab or workspace change (observations section 10), so a mirror that waited to be told would hold a tree for a tab nobody can reach. It goes without its own change: the tab's removal already says everything a reader needs, and a second announcement about a tab that no longer exists is a message with nowhere to land.

cases.name: a tree for a tab nobody has mentioned is kept
cases.why: herdr announces a new tab's layout and its tab with separate events, and nothing promises an order. A mirror that dropped a tree for arriving early would replace it with nothing until the next pane change, which on a tab where nobody is typing is never - so the tab would render empty for as long as it stayed quiet.

cases.name: a reconnect that finds a different tree says so
cases.why: Structure changing while a client was disconnected leaves no evidence at all - nothing reports a pane created and closed inside a gap - so the fresh snapshot is the only detector, and it has to report what moved rather than 'everything'. A reconnect that repainted every surface would make dropping the connection visibly expensive, and one that reported nothing would leave the window at the shape it had before the gap.

cases.name: a tab whose tree stopped reading keeps rendering
cases.why: A snapshot whose layout will not read - herdr moved a field, or sent rectangles that describe no tree - drops that tab's entry rather than the whole snapshot. The mirror reports the loss so a window can say the shape it is showing is old, and keeps the last tree, because a tab rendered as its previous arrangement is wrong in a way a user can see through and a tab rendered as nothing is not.

cases.name: an answer is applied like an event, and says the tab moved
cases.why: A daemon says things two ways - broadcast, and in reply to a request - and both are the daemon. herdr answers a swap with the settled tree in about a millisecond and publishes the same tree about a hundred milliseconds later (observations section 14), so a mirror that only listens spends six frames at 60fps rendering the arrangement it is moving away from. Taking the answer is the difference between a leftward split that lands and one that lands twice.

cases.name: an answer overtaken by a second one drops the broadcast in between
cases.why:
A resize chord held down, which is where this bites. Each repeat is answered before the previous one is broadcast, so the mirror is two arrangements ahead of its own stream and the broadcast that arrives describes where the divider was rather than where it is. Applying it walks the divider backwards one step per event.

The first answer arms nothing - the tab reached 0.5 by being told, so nothing is still owed for it. The second arms the first, because the backend has not got round to announcing that one yet. What separates the two is the debt, not the recency.

cases.name: an intermediate arrangement nobody asked for is dropped
cases.why: The case the whole thing exists for. herdr has no leftward split, so one is a rightward split followed by a swap, and it publishes both arrangements - 100.4 ms apart, measured (corpus/herdr-0.8.0/split-sides). Only the adapter knows what the middle one looked like, because only it issued the two halves, so it hands that tree over with the answer. Two arrangements are armed here rather than one: the tab's own previous tree, and the one published between the halves.

cases.name: an answer arriving after its own broadcast changes nothing
cases.why: Idempotence across the two channels. The event stream can win the race, and then the answer is stating what the mirror already holds - which is not news, and must not be reported as a change, or every split would repaint the tab twice. Nothing is armed either: a tab already where the daemon says it should be has no earlier arrangement still on its way.

cases.name: suppression is spent once, not standing
cases.why: What keeps this from being a mute button. An arrangement is dropped once and then forgotten, so a tab that genuinely comes back to that shape - somebody dragging a divider back, another client swapping the pair again - renders it. The alternative, suppressing until the expected tree turns up, is unbounded: nothing guarantees it ever does, and a window stuck on a stale arrangement is worse than one frame of the wrong one.

cases.name: an answer's broadcast arriving first does not clear the other one
cases.why: Order-independence, and why nothing is cleared for failing to match. The settled tree and the intermediate one are both in flight, and a mirror that dropped its guard on the first non-matching layout would then apply the intermediate and end up showing the pane on the side nobody asked for. Matching drains an entry; not matching leaves every entry alone.

cases.name: an arrangement is left behind whatever cursor came with it
cases.why: Why suppression names the tree rather than the whole layout. herdr's swap puts daemon focus on the source pane, so the arrangement it publishes between the halves of a leftward split names the *new* pane as focused and the one it settles on names the pane that was split - measured live, and the reason a first attempt at this let the flash straight through. Whole-layout equality would have called those two different things; they are the same arrangement, and the arrangement is what a person sees jump.

cases.name: a shape a tab comes back to is not an old answer arriving late
cases.why: The bound that keeps suppression from eating real news, and a bug this caught in the running app. Splitting upward settles a tab from `w1:p3` to `rows(w1:p6, w1:p3)`; closing the new pane collapses it straight back to `w1:p3`, and herdr broadcasts that - it is the only thing that says the pane is gone. An arrangement is only worth suppressing while the backend still owes a broadcast of it, and the tab reached `w1:p3` by being told, so that debt was paid long ago. Arming it regardless left a closed pane on screen with no way to dismiss it, because the tree the view was withholding still named a pane the tab no longer held.

cases.name: a state read after subscribing fills in what the stream never delivered
cases.why: herdr delivers agent state only to a subscriber that names the pane, and a watcher has to be told the pane exists before it can name it - so between a pane appearing and its watcher connecting there is a window, and herdr has no replay for what falls in it. A pane whose agent moved in that window keeps its old state and looks calm, which is this project's whole reason for existing failing silently at the moment it matters most: right after a split, with something new started in the pane. So the watcher subscribes and then asks.

cases.name: a read is refused when the stream moved the pane while the question was in flight
cases.why: The ordering rule, and the reason the caller passes what it believed. A live subscription is a better authority than an answer to a question asked at the same moment: the event was delivered because the daemon witnessed the transition, where the read is a snapshot of some instant the caller cannot pin down. So anything that arrives while the question is out wins, and the answer is dropped rather than applied over it.

cases.name: a read that agrees with what is already held changes nothing
cases.why: The ordinary case, and it has to be silent. Every watcher asks on every connection, so a read that reported a change whenever it merely confirmed one would flash every indicator in the window each time a subscription rebuilt - which is exactly what a reconnect does to every pane at once.

cases.name: a read recovers a finish the stream missed, not just a start
cases.why: The second shape the bug takes, and the one a rule about `unknown` alone would not catch. A pane can be `working` in the bootstrap snapshot and finish inside the window before its watcher is live - so the mirror holds a real state, not an absent one, and it is still wrong. Both were measured on the same flaky test, at two different transitions.

cases.name: a read for a pane the mirror does not hold is dropped
cases.why: A watcher outlives its pane by a moment: the pane closes, the read is already out, and the answer comes back about something nothing can place. Inventing a pane from it would produce an orphan with no tab and no workspace, which is the same refusal an agent event already gets and for the same reason.

cases.name: a read is refused when the caller believed the pane had no state at all
cases.why: Absent and `unknown` are different beliefs and the difference decides this. A caller with no belief never saw the pane, so it has nothing to compare against and no business writing over whatever the mirror learned in the meantime - where a caller that read `unknown` did look, and is entitled to say so.

cases.name: a tab whose last pane goes is a tab the backend has already closed
cases.why: Measured against herdr 0.8.0 rather than assumed: closing the only pane in a tab emits `pane_closed` and never a `tab_closed`, and `tab.list` stops reporting that tab from the same moment. So the tab is gone and nothing says so - a mirror that waited for an announcement would hold it forever. What that looks like on screen is a sidebar caption over no rows, and a region still pointed at a tab nobody can reach.

cases.name: a tab that still holds a pane survives losing one
cases.why: The other half, and the one that says this is an inference about emptiness rather than about removal. Closing one pane of a split leaves the tab exactly where it was, and a rule that dropped a tab on any pane removal would close a tab every time somebody closed a split.

cases.name: a pane removed as a tab's orphan does not remove the tab a second time
cases.why: `tab_closed` removes the tab and its panes with it, and each of those removals lands in the same place as an ordinary one. Without the guard the last orphan would infer that its tab is empty and try to remove it again - a second `tabRemoved` for one closing, and a recursion into a removal already in flight.

cases.name: a pane whose tab this mirror never learned takes no tab with it
cases.why: A pane arrives before its tab does - measured on herdr's own creation events, where `pane_created` precedes `tab_created` for the same tab. So a pane can be removed while its tab is still unknown here, and there is nothing to infer about a tab nobody has been told exists.

cases.name: a name and a title arrive on a pane and are reported once
cases.why:
The two better things a sidebar row can say than `directory · harness`. A name is what somebody called this pane and a title is what its program last called itself; herdr keeps them as separate fields and setting one never touches the other (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 16), so a pane can carry both and a row can show both.

One change rather than two, because a row is redrawn once whatever moved on it.

cases.name: a replayed pane does not clear a name or a title
cases.why:
The measured reason this is not simply 'apply what arrived'. herdr's replay is a ring buffer of past events rather than a fresh statement of the world, so reconnecting replays the pane's *creation* payload - which carries neither field, because neither existed when the pane was made. That replay is drained after the snapshot rather than before it, so treating an absent field as a clear would wipe every name and every title in the window on each reconnect.

Same fence as agent state, for the same reason and from the same recording (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 16). What it costs is stated where the code makes the choice: a title a program genuinely clears lingers until the next title change or the next snapshot.

cases.name: a snapshot is allowed to drop a name a pane no longer has
cases.why: The other half of the rule above, and what keeps it from being a leak. Clearing a name is real - `pane.rename` takes a null label and answers with a pane that has none - and a snapshot is a fresh statement of the whole world rather than a replayed fragment, so it is the one payload that may say a field is gone. Without this a cleared name would be unclearable for the life of the connection.

cases.name: a replayed pane does not put back a name the snapshot moved past
cases.why:
Found in the running app, with every layer under it green. A pane renamed from another client showed its *old* name in the window, and stayed wrong.

The absent-means-keep rule above is only half the defence. herdr's replay is a ring buffer of past events, and a subscription's replay is drained *after* the snapshot rather than before it - so what arrives is not a payload missing the fields, it is a payload carrying what they used to say. Keeping it would be applying an event the mirror has already moved past.

`revision` is the ordering that settles it, and it is herdr's own: it counts terminal titles and metadata tokens, which is exactly these two fields and nothing else (observations/herdr-0.8.0.md sections 10 and 16). A payload older than what is held says nothing about either field. It is deliberately not a general fence - cwd and the harness are not what revision counts, so they still take the newest thing that arrived.
